name: Triathlon nutrition
seoDesc: Triathlon nutrition: work out distance from the target time and the swimming time. A free sports calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Supply the target time, the swimming time, the cycling time and the running time and the Triathlon nutrition calculator solves for distance. It suits a training session, a performance comparison or a competition result. Nothing is submitted anywhere: the arithmetic runs in the page you are looking at.

sections.title: How does the Triathlon nutrition calculator work?
sections.html:
The Triathlon nutrition calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports distance in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the sport, the triathlon type and the time per sport); then you type in the target time, the swimming time, the cycling time and the running time.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Triathlon nutrition calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Distance=(1 ÷ 60) × speed × target time
Calories training=(speed, your weight, target time, sport)
Calories replaced=((1 ÷ 4) × (speed, your weight, target time, sport))
Calories triathlon=(target time, triathlon type, your weight)
Calories triathlon custom=(swimming time, cycling time, running time, triathlon type, your weight)
Speed warning=(speed, I am, sport)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Length, opening in kilometers
  • Time, opening in hours / minutes
  • Time, opening in minutes / seconds
  • Time, opening in minutes / seconds
  • Time, opening in minutes / seconds
  • Mass, opening in kilograms
  • Volume, opening in milliliters

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Triathlon nutrition calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Comparing two athletes or two attempts fairly
  • Planning a session around a target you already know
  • Tracking progress across a training block
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the target time, the swimming time and the cycling time — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Triathlon nutrition calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns distance, derived from the target time, the swimming time and the cycling time. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Triathlon nutrition calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the target time, the swimming time, the cycling time and the running time, which is 10 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter distance in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Distance opens in kilometers and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (4 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Distance = 0 km. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Triathlon nutrition calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
